title: 1 Samuel 17:31–40
context: David’s words reach Saul, and David volunteers to fight. Saul objects that he is only a youth, but David tells how the LORD delivered him from the lion and the bear and expresses confidence that the LORD will deliver him from the Philistine. Saul tries to arm David with his own armor, which David cannot use. David goes out with his staff, his sling and five smooth stones from the brook. The section contrasts trust grounded in the LORD’s past faithfulness with reliance on royal equipment. Both traditions see David’s faith as real trust in the living God, shaped by experience of his deliverance. Neither tradition draws a doctrine from the number of stones; readers have offered various explanations, and the text itself does not explain the choice.

verses.text: When the words were heard which David spoke, they rehearsed them before Saul; and he sent for him.
verses.arminianNotes:
David’s words are reported to Saul, who sends for him. The private conversation becomes a royal summons.

Arminian readers note that David’s spoken faith has public consequences; what he says reaches the king, showing that a believer’s words can stir others when they express trust in God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God brings his chosen one before the king through the report of others, and that this verse is the last of the stretch (17:12–31) lacking in the shorter Septuagint form, a reminder of the textual questions in this chapter.

Both traditions see the summons as a turning point in which David’s faith moves from words to action.

verses.text: David said to Saul, “Let no man’s heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David tells Saul that no one should lose heart because of Goliath, for he, Saul’s servant, will go and fight. He offers himself.

Arminian readers note that David volunteers freely, and that this willing self-offering is the response of faith God desires; he does not wait to be compelled but steps forward.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s courage is the fruit of the Spirit who came on him at his anointing (16:13), so that his willingness is itself God’s gift working through his own resolve.

Both traditions affirm both that David truly chooses and that his courage rests on the LORD, though they describe the relation between grace and willing differently.

verses.text: Saul said to David, “You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him; for you are but a youth, and he a man of war from his youth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul says David cannot fight Goliath, since he is only a youth and Goliath has been a warrior from his youth. Saul’s assessment is reasonable by human standards.

Arminian readers note that Saul sees only human capacities and leaves God out of the calculation, which mirrors the unbelief that led to his rejection (13:13–14; 15:22–23).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s objection measures strength by experience and stature, while the story will show that God chooses the weak to shame the strong, a pattern Paul later describes (1 Corinthians 1:27).

Both traditions see Saul’s realism as a foil for David’s faith.

verses.text: David said to Saul, “Your servant was keeping his father’s sheep; and when a lion or a bear came and took a lamb out of the flock,
verses.arminianNotes:
David tells Saul that while keeping his father’s sheep, a lion or a bear would come and take a lamb from the flock. He begins to recount his experience.

Arminian readers note that David’s past faithfulness in protecting the sheep was a real choice to risk himself, and that each act of trust strengthened his readiness for a greater test.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s shepherd experience was part of God’s preparation, ordained long before this day, so that David could testify to the LORD’s past faithfulness when the crisis came.

Both traditions read David’s shepherd testimony as evidence of God’s prior deliverance and of David’s growing trust.

verses.text: I went out after him, struck him, and rescued it out of his mouth. When he arose against me, I caught him by his beard, struck him, and killed him.
verses.arminianNotes:
David says he went after the predator, struck it, rescued the lamb from its mouth, and when it attacked him, seized it by the beard and killed it. The account shows courage and protective care.

Arminian readers note that David acted as a shepherd who risks himself for the sheep, displaying the kind of costly love that God calls his servants to choose.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the image of a shepherd rescuing sheep from a predator’s mouth echoes later prophetic and gospel language of God’s shepherding care (Ezekiel 34:10–12; John 10:11), though David’s account is first a literal story.

Both traditions see here a portrait of the shepherd heart God values in a king.

verses.text: Your servant struck both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, since he has defied the armies of the living God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David says he has killed both lion and bear, and the uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them because he has defied the armies of the living God. David links past deliverance with present confidence.

Arminian readers note that David’s confidence is not presumption but reasoned trust based on God’s faithfulness, and that faith grows through remembering what God has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David grounds his expectation on Goliath’s defiance of the living God, so his confidence rests on God’s commitment to his own name rather than on David’s skill.

Both traditions agree that David’s courage is faith in the living God, not self-confidence.

verses.text: David said, “The LORD, who delivered me out of the paw of the lion and out of the paw of the bear, will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.” Saul said to David, “Go! The LORD will be with you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
David says the LORD who delivered him from lion and bear will deliver him from the Philistine, and Saul tells him to go, with the LORD’s presence. David names the LORD as the deliverer.

Arminian readers note that David attributes every past victory to God, and that Saul, though rejected, can still speak a blessing, showing God’s grace even through flawed leaders.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s testimony is explicitly theological: the LORD delivered, and the LORD will deliver, so the coming victory is credited in advance to God and not to David’s hand.

Both traditions treat David’s words as a clear confession of trust in the LORD’s saving power.

verses.text: Saul dressed David with his clothing. He put a helmet of bronze on his head, and he clad him with a coat of mail.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul dresses David in his own clothing, a bronze helmet and a coat of mail. The king tries to equip David in his own image.

Arminian readers note that Saul’s gesture may be well meant, yet it reflects his reliance on human means, which David must choose whether to accept or set aside.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Saul’s armor symbolizes the strength of the old regime, which God does not need; the LORD will work through his chosen servant without the trappings of Saul’s kingship.

Both traditions see the scene as testing whether David will trust in borrowed armor or in the LORD.

verses.text: David strapped his sword on his clothing and he tried to move, for he had not tested it. David said to Saul, “I can’t go with these, for I have not tested them.” Then David took them off.
verses.arminianNotes:
David straps on Saul’s sword and tries to walk, but having never tested the equipment, he tells Saul he cannot go with it and takes it off. David chooses familiar means.

Arminian readers note that David exercises practical wisdom, choosing what he knows how to use, and that faith does not reject sensible judgment but works through it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s laying aside the armor highlights that God’s victories do not depend on royal equipment, though David still uses ordinary means; God works through means without being bound to the strongest ones.

Both traditions agree that faith and practical wisdom work together here.

verses.text: He took his staff in his hand, and chose for himself five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in the pouch of his shepherd’s bag which he had. His sling was in his hand; and he came near to the Philistine.
verses.arminianNotes:
David takes his staff, chooses five smooth stones from the brook, puts them in his shepherd’s bag, and approaches Goliath with sling in hand. He goes as a shepherd.

Arminian readers note that the text does not explain why David took five stones, and readers should avoid building doctrines on the number; preparing sensibly is compatible with trusting God fully.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that various explanations for the five stones have been offered, but the text is silent, and the detail is best not pressed; the emphasis falls on a shepherd’s ordinary weapon used in reliance on God.

Both traditions share this caution and see no doctrinal disagreement over the stones.
